summary: The latest in a series of revisions of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 10, RFC 16, RFC 24 and RFC 27. It restates how notes are written and shared in the series.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the newest version of the group's rules for writing and sharing notes.

questions: what is a network working group note
what is the minimum length of an early rfc
subtitle: The early rules for writing and circulating Network Working Group notes: be timely, not polished.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group needed a simple way for people at ARPA network sites to share ideas about HOST software, without people feeling that a written note had to be authoritative or polished.
tldr.mechanism: Notes may come from anybody at any site and be about any thought related to the network. Each note carries a standard header and one copy is mailed from the author's site to a short list of 14 people.
tldr.outcome: RFC 30 is a revision of RFC 10, 16, 24 and 27. It sets the informal tone of the note series: the minimum length of a note is one sentence.

today: The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 30, and its status is recorded as Unknown. It is itself a revision of RFC 10, RFC 16, RFC 24 and RFC 27.

sections.title: The Network Working Group and Its Notes
sections.content:
RFC 30, dated 4 February 1970 and written by S. Crocker of UCLA, is a revision of NWG/RFC 10, 16, 24 and 27. The Network Working Group (NWG) consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites, and membership is not closed.

The group is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network. Its work is documented through notes like this one. Notes may be produced at any site by anybody and included in the series.
sections.plainLanguage: A group of people who want computers to talk to each other write short notes to share ideas. Anyone who is interested can join in and write one.

sections.title: What a Note May Contain
sections.content:
The content of a note may be any thought or suggestion related to the HOST software or other aspect of the network. Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples, suggestions without background, and explicit questions without any attempted answers are all acceptable. The minimum length for a note is one sentence.

The RFC says why these standards, or lack of them, are stated explicitly. First, people tend to treat anything written as authoritative, and the group wants to promote the exchange of ideas that are far less than authoritative. Second, people hesitate to publish something unpolished, and the group hopes to ease that inhibition.
sections.plainLanguage: You can share a half-finished idea. Nobody expects a note to be perfect, and even one sentence counts.

sections.title: Required Form and Distribution
sections.content:
Every note should bear four things: the words "Network Working Group" and "Request for Comments: X" where X is a serial number, the author and affiliation, the date, and a title. Serial numbers are assigned by Steve Crocker at UCLA, and the title need not be unique.

For distribution, one copy only is sent from the author's site to each of 14 named people at sites including MIT, Utah, SDC, UCLA, SRI, MITRE, Carnegie-Mellon, RAND, BB&N, Raytheon, ARPA, Lincoln Laboratory, Stanford and UCSB. Reproduction, if desired, may be handled locally. The RFC ends with the most current postal addresses and phone numbers of those people, and asks readers to correct them as necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note gets a number, a name, a date and a title. Then the author mails one copy to each of 14 people, and they can make more copies themselves.
